# Background

The study investigated whether frequency constellations of food health and taste in different contexts contribute to beliefs about the health-taste relationship. We hypothesised that if there is more tasty and unhealthy food in one than another context, people will perceive an unhealthy-tasty relationship, regardless of the actual contingency between health and taste. Conversely, if there is more tasty and healthy food in one than another context, people will perceive a healthy-tasty relationship.

## Procedure

Participants viewed health and taste ratings of individual foods from two different contexts, specifically "cafeterias at the workplace" and "restaurants in the area". Afterwards, they indicated to what extent they perceived a relationship between health and taste, separately in each context, as well as overall, across contexts.

## Design 

6 conditions in a mixed design. Each participant viewed information about food from two contexts (within factor `context`). Participants were randomly assigned to the `harmonious`, `conflicting` or `control` base rate manipulation (between factor `condition`). In the `harmonious` base rate manipulation, there were both more healthy and tasty foods in the first than the second context. In the `conflicting` base rate manipulation, there were more unhealthy and tasty foods in the first than the second context. In the `control` group, there were just as many tasty as non tasty and healthy as unhealthy foods in both contexts.

The contexts had different names and background colours which were counter-balanced between participants (variables `random_context` and `random_colour`). 

## Dependent measures

The dependent variable was participants’ perceived relationship between healthiness and tastiness, which we assessed in three ways: 

Participants estimated for each context, how many of the healthy meals were tasty and not tasty and how many of the unhealthy meals were tasty and not tasty (Joint frequency estimates). Out of these four estimates, we calculated the phi coefficient per context and participant.

Also, participants indicated, within each context as well as across contexts, whether they believe the healthy foods to be less healthy, equally healthy or healthier than unhealthy foods and vice versa, on a slider scale ranging from 1-100 (Contingency belief). We subsequently re-coded these items so that they ranged from - .5 to .5. 

In addition, participants predicted the taste rating of new meals from both contexts based on their given health rating and vice versa (Prediction task). We calculated the Pearson correlation coefficient between the given and predicted ratings per context and participant.

We averaged these three measures into one index for the perceived relationship between health and taste within each context.

The data processing steps are documented in a separate R markdown file: `Study2_processing.Rmd`.

## Attention/Manipulation checks and additional measures

To ensure that participants paid attention to the presented health and taste ratings, we asked them to recall each rating on a scale from 1 = *not tasty/healthy at all* to 5 = *very tasty/healthy* (On-line ratings).

To ensure that participants recognized the skewed frequencies of healthy and tasty food across the different contexts, they estimated how many foods per context were (un)healthy and (not) tasty, respectively (Base rate estimates).

The manipulation check analyses are documented in a separate R markdown file: `Study2_manipulation_checks.Rmd`.

Additionally, we assessed participants general (un)healthy = tasty belief (UTI), and general health interest (GHI) to control for their possible influence in the analyses. For the control analyses, see the separate R markdown file `Study2_control.Rmd`.

Load required packages:
```{r, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(misty)
library(ggplot2)
library(jtools)
library(rstatix)
library(knitr)
library(Rmisc)
```
Import processed data.
```{r}
dat <- read.csv2('Data/Study2_data_processed.csv')
```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Turn the id and group variables into factors and add labels to the groups.
dat <-
  dat %>% 
  mutate(id = factor(id),
         condition = factor(condition, 
                            levels = c('1', '2', '3'), 
                            labels = c('Harmonious', 'Conflicting', 'Control'))
  )
```

# Perceived health-taste relationship within contexts

First, we tested the effects of base rate manipulation, context and their interaction on the participants' perceived health-taste relationship. 
We calculated a mixed ANOVA, testing the effect of the between-subjects factor base rate manipulation (harmonious vs. conflicting vs. control), within-subjects factor context (1st vs. 2nd) and their interaction on the perceived health-taste relationship. We expected a significant main effect of base rate manipulation.

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Restructure data from wide into long format for the mixed ANOVA, convert the context variable into a factor.
dat_long <-
  dat %>% 
  select(id, condition, ht_rel_c1, ht_rel_c2) %>% 
  pivot_longer(cols = c('ht_rel_c1', 'ht_rel_c2'), 
                       names_to = 'context',
                       values_to = 'ht_rel') %>% 
  mutate(context = rec(context, '"ht_rel_c1" = 1; "ht_rel_c2" = 2')) %>%
  mutate(context =factor(context,
                         levels = c('1', '2'),
                         labels= c('1st Context', '2nd Context')))
```
  
## Descriptive statistics

```{r, echo=FALSE}
# Check the mean, standard deviation, standard error and 95% confidence interval of the perceived health-taste relationship in each base rate manipulation and context.
ht_rel_sum <- summarySE(dat_long, measurevar='ht_rel', groupvars=c('condition', 'context'))
ht_rel_sum %>% 
  kable(format = 'markdown', digits = 2,
        col.names = c('Base rate manipulation', 'Context','N', 'Mean relationship', 'Std. Dev.', 'Std. Error', '95% CI'), 
        caption = 'Mean perceived health-taste relationship by base rate manipulation and context')

```
## ANOVA
```{r}
aov_ht_rel <-
  anova_test(
  data = dat_long, dv = ht_rel, wid = id,
  between = condition, within = context, type = 3, effect.size = 'pes')
```
```{r, echo=FALSE}
options(dplyr.summarise.inform = FALSE) # Deactivate the warning message
colnames(aov_ht_rel) <- c('Effect','df/nominator', 'df/denominator', '$F$', '$p$', 'Sig.', 'partial $\\eta^2$')
rownames(aov_ht_rel) <- c('Base rate manipulation', 'Context', 'Base rate manipulation*Context')
kable(aov_ht_rel[,-1],format = 'markdown',  digits = 2,
      caption = 'Results of the ANOVA testing the effect of base rate manipulation and context on the perceived health-taste relationship')
```

As expected, there was a large main effect of base rate manipulation. There was also a small effect of the 2-way interaction between base rate manipulation and context. To follow up, we calculated pairwise comparisons between base rate manipulations within each context.

### Pairwise comparisons

```{r, echo=FALSE}
ht_rel_pw <- 
  dat_long %>%
  group_by(context) %>% 
  pairwise_t_test(ht_rel ~ condition, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")

kable(ht_rel_pw[,-c(2, 5, 6)], format = 'markdown', digits = 2,
        caption = 'Pairwise comparisons of the perceived health-taste relationship between base rate manipulations within each context',
        col.names = c('Context', 'Base rate manipulation 1', 'Base rate manipulation 2',  '$p$', 'Sign', '$p.adj$', 'Sign. adj.'))
```

In the second context with many not tasty foods, there was no difference in the perceived health-taste relationship between the harmonious base rate manipulation and control group. Otherwise, the perceived health-taste relationship differed between all base rate manipulations in both contexts.

## Plot the results

To illustrate that the perceived health-taste relationship was even opposite to the actual contingency, we plotted both the actual and perceived health-taste relationship within the different base rate manipulations and contexts.

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Restructure both real and perceived contingency into long format
dat_realcor <-
  dat %>% 
  select('id', 'condition', starts_with(c('ht_rel', 'real'))) %>% 
  pivot_longer(-c('id', 'condition'),
               names_to = 'trial',
               values_to = 'cor') %>% 
  mutate(context = case_when(grepl('c1', trial) ~ 1,
                             grepl('c2', trial, ignore.case = TRUE) ~ 2),
         
         realness = ifelse(str_detect(trial, fixed('real')), 1, 2) 
         ) %>% 
  mutate(context =factor(context,
                         levels = c('1', '2'),
                         labels= c('1st Context', '2nd Context')),
         realness = factor(realness,
                           levels = c('1', '2'),
                           labels = c('Real Relationship', 'Perceived Relationship'))
  ) 

```

```{r, include=FALSE}
# Calculate the mean, standard deviation, standard error and 95% confidence interval of the real and perceived health-taste relationship in each base rate manipulation and context, for plotting.
realcor_sum <- summarySE(dat_realcor, measurevar='cor', groupvars=c('condition', 'context', 'realness'))
```

```{r,echo=FALSE}
# Plot the real and perceived health-taste relationship by base rate manipulation and context, with CIs
realcor_sum %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=condition, y=cor, fill=context)) + 
  geom_bar(position=position_dodge(), stat="identity") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=cor-ci, ymax=cor+ci),
                width=.2,                   
                position=position_dodge(.9)) +
  facet_wrap('realness') +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-.50, .50))+
  theme_apa() +
  labs(x = 'Base Rate Manipulation', y = 'Mean Relationship')+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.position = 'top')

```

# Perceived health-taste relationship across contexts

Next, we tested the effects of base rate manipulation on participants' perceived health-taste relationship (Contingency belief) across contexts, with a one-way ANOVA.
  
## Descriptive statistics

```{r, echo=FALSE}

# Check the mean, standard deviation, standard error and 95% confidence interval of the perceived health-taste relationship across contexts in each base rate manipulation.
beliefov_sum <- summarySE(dat, measurevar= 'belief_ht_overall_R', groupvars='condition')

beliefov_sum %>% 
  kable(format = 'markdown', digits = 2,
        col.names = c('Context','N', 'Mean relationship', 'Std. Dev.', 'Std. Error', '95% CI'), 
        caption = 'Mean perceived health-taste relationship by base rate manipulation')

```
## ANOVA

```{r, message=FALSE}
aov_belief_ov <-
  anova_test(
    data = dat, dv = belief_ht_overall_R,
    between = condition, type = 3, effect.size = 'pes')

```

```{r, echo=FALSE}

colnames(aov_belief_ov) <- c('Effect','df/nominator', 'df/denominator', '$F$', '$p$', 'Sig.', 'partial $\\eta^2$')
rownames(aov_belief_ov) <- 'Base rate manipulation'

kable(aov_belief_ov[,-1], format = 'markdown',  digits = 2,
      caption = 'Results of the ANOVA testing the effect of base rate manipulation on the perceived health-taste relationship across contexts')
```

### Pairwise comparisons 

As expected, there was a large main effect of base rate manipulation. To follow up, we calculated pairwise comparisons between all three base rate manipulations.

### Pairwise comparisons

```{r, echo=FALSE}
beliefov_pw <- 
  dat %>%
  pairwise_t_test(belief_ht_overall_R ~ condition, p.adjust.method = "bonferroni")

kable(beliefov_pw[,-c(1, 4:5)], format = 'markdown', digits = 2,
        caption = 'Pairwise comparisons of the perceived health-taste relationship across contexts between base rate manipulations',
        col.names = c('Base rate manipulation 1', 'Base rate manipulation 2', '$p$', 'Sign', '$p.adj$', 'Sign. adj.'))
```

The perceived health-taste relationship differed between all base rate manipulations, except the harmonious base rates and control group.

## Plot the results

```{r, echo=FALSE}
beliefov_sum %>%
  ggplot(aes(x=condition, y=belief_ht_overall_R, fill=condition)) + 
  geom_bar(position=position_dodge(), stat="identity") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin=belief_ht_overall_R-ci, ymax=belief_ht_overall_R+ci),
                width=.2,                   
                position=position_dodge(.9)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0)+
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.25, 0.25))+
  theme_apa() +
  labs(x = 'Base Rate Manipulation', y = 'Mean Relationship')+
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
        legend.position = 'none',
        axis.title.y = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 18),
        axis.title.x = element_text(face = 'bold', size = 18),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 18),
        text = element_text(size = 16)) 
```

# Summary of results

Within as well as across contexts, participants viewing harmonious base rates perceived a healthy-tasty relationship, whereas participants viewing conflicting base rates perceived an unhealthy-tasty relationship, despite actual opposite contingencies within and zero contingencies across contexts. Participants in the control group estimated the relationship to be close to zero, with a trend towards a healthy-tasty relationship.
